name: Dual-plane breast augmentation

card.summary: A breast implant pocket technique in which the upper part of the implant sits under the chest muscle and the lower part sits behind breast tissue, used to shape the upper and lower breast contour.
card.note: Surgical procedure with implant-related complications such as capsular contracture and implant movement with muscle contraction.

quick.overview:
Dual-plane augmentation is a way of positioning a breast implant. Part of the implant is covered by the pectoralis major muscle, and the lower portion lies in the plane behind the breast gland. Surgeons describe it as a way to combine soft upper-pole coverage with room for the lower breast to fill out, which is how people use it to shape a rounder, more natural-looking breast outline.

It became one of the two most common implant pockets alongside the subglandular position, and it has been the standard approach in implant-based reconstruction for decades. Published work is mostly surgical reviews and case series, with a few randomized comparisons of surgical details.
quick.how: The procedure is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia through an incision in the breast crease, around the areola, in the armpit (sometimes with an endoscope) or, rarely, at the navel. The surgeon releases the lower attachments of the pectoralis muscle so the implant sits partly beneath it. Surgeons choose the amount of release according to breast type, and recovery plans are set by the operating surgeon.
quick.risks: Reported complications of breast augmentation include capsular contracture (the most common), implant malposition, asymmetry and scarring. Placing implants beneath the muscle is associated with animation deformity, in which the implant shifts when the chest muscle contracts, and with a more painful early recovery than subglandular placement. Regulators such as the FDA have issued warnings about textured implants and BIA-ALCL, and implants are not lifetime devices.

lead: Dual-plane breast augmentation is a surgical technique for positioning a breast implant so that its upper portion lies beneath the pectoralis major muscle while its lower portion lies in front of the muscle, behind the breast tissue.[1] People who choose it do so to change breast size and shape, and surgeons describe the arrangement as giving the upper part of the implant muscle coverage while letting the lower breast expand over the implant.[1]

Reviews list the subpectoral dual-plane and the subglandular positions as the two most common implant pockets for cosmetic augmentation, usually reached through an incision under the breast, around the areola or in the armpit.[2] In reconstruction after mastectomy, the dual-plane approach was for about two decades the most frequently performed way to place an implant, until prepectoral placement began to be used in selected patients.[3]

Research on the technique consists mainly of surgical technique papers, reviews and comparative studies. A 2001 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described dual-plane augmentation as a way to optimize implant and soft-tissue relationships across a wide range of breast types, and a later 2006 paper revisited it.[4][5] Documented concerns include capsular contracture, animation deformity and early postoperative pain.[1][3]

chain: Implant placed partly under the pectoralis muscle
Muscle covers the upper pole while the lower pole is released
Softer upper contour with a filled lower breast
angle.text: The technique is used to change how an implant sits and shows. Muscle coverage over the upper part is intended to soften the upper edge of the implant, while releasing the muscle's lower attachments lets the lower pole fill the breast shape.

paras: Implants can be placed in front of the pectoralis major (subglandular or subfascial), fully beneath it (submuscular), or partly beneath it in the dual-plane arrangement; in some reconstructions they are placed above the muscle, called prepectoral.[6] In a dual-plane pocket the surgeon releases the muscle's lower attachments so that the upper implant is under muscle and the lower implant is in contact with the breast gland.[6]

Descriptions of the 2001 technique emphasize adjusting how much of the implant is covered according to breast and tissue characteristics, so that the implant relates differently to the lower breast depending on the patient.[4]

Implants for augmentation are reached through the inframammary fold, the areola's lower edge, the armpit or the navel; the axillary route is described as the preferred incision for Asian women in one review, which discusses an endoscope-assisted high-position dual-plane technique.[2][7]

Subglandular placement is described as sitting closest to natural breast tissue, but in thin tissue, ripples may show and capsular contracture is somewhat more common; fully submuscular placement is rarely used cosmetically because of animation deformity.[6] Dual-plane is presented as a middle option that balances those factors.[6]

In reconstruction, reviews report that some patients with dual-plane implants had pain and animation deformity from muscle manipulation, and prepectoral placement, often with acellular dermal matrix, has been used to avoid these in selected patients with results reported as similar.[3][8]

Capsular contracture, in which scar tissue tightens around an implant, is reported as the most common complication after breast augmentation and a leading reason for revision surgery.[2][9] Antimicrobial technique, matrices and scaffolds, and prepectoral positioning have been studied for prevention.[9]

Other documented issues include implant malposition, asymmetry, distortion with muscle movement, scarring and changes in nipple sensation. A study assessing breast distortion after submuscular augmentation examined how muscle activity alters breast appearance.[10] Regulators have also issued warnings about BIA-ALCL linked to textured implants.[6]

Published studies are mostly case series, reviews and technique comparisons. A randomized trial compared harmonic scalpel with monopolar cautery in transaxillary endoscopic dual-plane augmentation.[11] A randomized trial in dual-plane immediate reconstruction compared synthetic and biological mesh within the same patients after five years of follow-up.[12] A Phase 1 registration also covers an endoscope-assisted axillary dual-plane approach.[13] Breast augmentation in general has not been associated with increased breast cancer risk in a review.[2]

timeline.event: Dual-plane augmentation described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery as a way to adapt implant coverage to different breast types.[4]
A follow-up paper on the technique appears in the same journal.[5]
Acellular dermis-assisted partial-submuscular (dual-plane equivalent) reconstruction reported.[14]
Prepectoral implant-based reconstruction reported as an option to avoid muscle-related animation deformity.[8]
